records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated S. truncata page renders an alphabetized seven-entry Common Name(s) list (Claw Cactus, Crab Cactus, Crab's Claw Cactus, False Christmas Cactus, Holiday Cactus, Lobster Cactus, Thanksgiving Cactus), in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and its description calls Thanksgiving the plant's most popular common name: 'The Thanksgiving cactus is a tough, epiphytic succulent that has showy flowers in the winter, usually around Thanksgiving, hence its most popular common name.' RHS's dedicated page is titled 'Schlumbergera truncata | Christmas cactus' and lists 'Christmas cactus, common winter cactus, crab cactus, lobster cactus' under Other common names. NC State lists Zygocactus truncatus (with Cactus truncatus and Epiphyllum truncatum) under 'Previously known as'. Thanksgiving Cactus was chosen because of the NC State description sentence.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Schlumbergera truncata page carries the tags '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs'. The full tag block reads: #showy flowers #interiorscape #succulent #red flowers #white flowers #pink flowers #yellow flowers #epiphytic #tough plant #winter interest #fantz #humidity tolerant #Christmas decorations #fleshy leaves #winter flowers #easy to grow #easy to propagate #houseplant #non-toxic for cats #herbaceous perennial #container plant #non-toxic for dogs #pet friendly #perennial #arching #hummingbird friendly #florist plant. Plant Type is four values: Epiphyte, Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Succulent. The page has no Poison block, no poisonous-part list, no symptom list, and no handling warning, so there is no human-scoped severity rating. The statement is a tag on this page, not a feeding trial or a toxicology citation. Edibility: the same page's Uses (Ethnobotany) line says 'Used for medicine, has environmental uses, and for food.' It names no plant part and gives no preparation, times or conditions. Do not read it as a safe-to-eat instruction. Other admissible pages found speak only at genus level (Penn State: 'Schlumbergera spp.', relaying the ASPCA) and were not used.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State's problems text says reduced flowering or dropping of flower buds can be from inadequate dark hours (at least 13 uninterrupted hours), sudden temperature changes, lack of moisture, or light changes. Its description also says the plant can be forced into blooming by night temperatures of 40 degrees for several successive nights. The page does not label these a formal rest period or give a duration for the cool exposure beyond 'several successive nights'.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org could not be loaded (certificate and connection errors), so no MoBot citation was made. UF/IFAS, Clemson (HTTP 403), UMD and UGA had no dedicated S. truncata page that was found or readable. Evidence is therefore NC State plus RHS only.
toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' tags on the S. truncata page. Penn State's genus-level 'Schlumbergera spp.' pet statement was not used.

is_edible left null: NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) field for this species reads 'Used for medicine, has environmental uses, and for food.' It names no plant part, preparation, dose, condition or grower's use, which is too vague to support true. The page has no Edibility field, and the RHS page says nothing about eating. The line is not a safe-to-eat statement.

NC State's description says 70 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit without saying day or night, so day and night temperature fields are null. The 40 degree night figure is a bloom-forcing trigger, not a night range.
chill_damage_f: no source states a damage-onset temperature. RHS's minimum temperature of 10C is a growing recommendation, and the RHS H1B rating is not an onset figure.

water_regime and the watering interval fields are null. For the established plant, NC State's only watering instruction is 'Avoid overwatering.'; its problems text adds 'Root rot can be a problem for overwatered plants.' and names lack of moisture as one cause of bud drop. Its 'water when the potting mix is completely dry' sentence is propagation advice for stem segments before they root ('The stems will take root after a few weeks.'). The Moist value in NC State's Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry) describes soil, not a watering cadence. Penn State's Holiday Cacti Care page ('When the medium becomes dry, water again.') covers three holiday cacti and was not used.

NC State's Light field reads 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', a site-wide legend, so direct_sun_hours_max is null. NC State prose says direct sunlight can scorch the stems. RHS Position is Partial shade.

Fertilizer: NC State says fertilize monthly once new growth starts in spring and reduce it in fall and early winter. Interval, months and strength are left null because no literal day count or dilution fraction is given.

soil_ph_max=8 is the closed top of NC State's 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band. RHS lists pH as 'Acid or Neutral' and does not list alkaline. soil_ph_min is null because NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended.

Size conflict: NC State gives 9-12 in height and 12-24 in width (prose: 'It grows up to 12 inches tall and 24 inches wide.'). RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in). NC State was used as the anchor. Houseplant size rule: neither page gives a separate indoor or container figure, and NC State's figures are well under 120 in, so they stand.
RHS's Hardiness field for this page shows H1B. NC State lists USDA zones 10a-12b. Neither is a damage-onset temperature.

Penn State's 'Holiday Cacti Care' page covers both Thanksgiving and Christmas cacti and gives 'at least twelve hours' of uninterrupted darkness, against NC State's 13 hours on the dedicated page. The Penn State page was not used for any field.

common_name: RHS's lead for this species, 'Christmas cactus', is the common_name this catalog already carries for Schlumbergera × buckleyi (b4-tricky-cases), so it could not be landed here in any case; NC State's description lead, Thanksgiving cactus, is used.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list for Euphorbia trigona is alphabetized (Abyssinian Euphorbia comes first) and its page-title parenthetical carries the same nine names comma-joined, including African Milk Tree. The RHS page for this exact name is titled 'Euphorbia trigona | African milk tree', and RHS's other-common-names field gives marble column. The names Candelabra Cactus, Cathedral Cactus, Friendship Cactus and Good Luck Cactus are on NC State's list, but NC State says the plant resembles a cactus and is a member of the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae). records.toxicity_detail: NC State, 'Poisonous to Humans' block (human-scoped): Poison Severity Medium. Poison Symptoms: 'The milky sap from the stems or leaves can cause skin irritation, rash, blisters, and severe eye irritation with contact. Severe gastroenteritis, vomiting, diarrhea, and convulsions can occur, if ingested.The milky sap is an irritant whether ingested or applied externally.' Poison Toxic Principle: diterpenoid euphorbol esters. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems. NC State's separate Problems field lists: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Spines/Thorns; the cat and dog tags are separate from the human-scoped Poison block and carry no severity rating or symptom list of their own. Plant Type values: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Poisonous, Shrub, Succulent, Tree. Tags on the page include #poisonous if ingested, #contact dermatitis, #spines, #problem for cats, #problem for dogs, #problem for children. NC State Edibility field: 'The sap is toxic and an irritant if ingested or handled.' Handling: 'Keep this plant out of the reach of pets and children due to its toxicity. Wear gloves when handling this plant due to the risk of skin irritation or blistering.' RHS (Potentially harmful, 'Humans/Pets' heading, no animal named): 'IRRITANT to skin/eye; harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.'

unknowns: Only two admissible sources were readable: NC State (dedicated Euphorbia trigona page) and RHS (dedicated page). The MoBot Plant Finder page (taxonid 280109) could not be fetched here (TLS/connect error from the sandbox), so nothing was taken from it. No dedicated page was found on Clemson (403), UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's separate 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs' tags only; those tags carry no symptom list or severity. The symptom list and Medium severity come from NC State's human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' block. RHS's warning is headed 'Humans/Pets' and names no animal.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State only says outdoor plants should be brought indoors before temperatures drop below 45 F, and its 'warm environment between 65 to 85 degrees Fahrenheit' sentence says 'Most species' and gives no day/night split, so day/night temperatures are null. RHS rates this species H2 (UK legend: tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen, 1 to 5 C), a hardiness rating, not a damage-onset figure. NC State USDA zones 9a-11b are a survival range, not an onset temperature.

soil_drainage left null: NC State gives only 'Good Drainage' plus prose 'well-drained, and sandy or loamy', and a 'dry soils tolerant' tag; RHS says only 'Well-drained'. No source calls for sharp, gritty drainage with no wet tolerance, so fast is not set, and a bare well-drained is ambiguous.
soil_ph left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) (open-ended acid band gives no floor), and RHS lists pH as acid or alkaline or neutral, so no ceiling can be set.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field is Partial Shade (mapped to part_shade); its prose says partial sun outdoors and bright indirect light indoors. RHS Position lists Full sun and Partial shade (UK-calibrated); full_sun is left out because NC State's structured field does not carry it. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the '2-6 hours' text is NC State's generic light-category legend.

water_regime dry_surface_between is read from NC State's species prose ('water sparingly', 'when the soil feels dry at the surface depth of 1 to 2 inches'); water_check_depth_cm 5 is the 2-inch end of that range. RHS gives 'Drought Resistance Yes' and 'Moisture Well-drained' only, no watering schedule. No source gives day-interval figures, so those are null. NC State also warns overwatering can cause root rot.
is_edible=false: NC State states the sap is toxic and an irritant if ingested, tags the plant #poisonous if ingested, and RHS says harmful if eaten. No source describes any edible use.

attracts_pollinators left null: NC State says the plant attracts insects, pollinators and small birds only 'in its native habitat' and that when cultivated it is not known for attracting any wildlife, so the claim is conditional.

Mature size left null at landing, all four fields (houseplant size rule: when the only figure is the outdoor stature and its height or spread exceeds 120 in with no indoor figure, the size stays null). NC State's Dimensions block reads 'Height: 6 ft. 0 in. - 12 ft. 0 in.' and 'Width: 5 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in.' (72-144 in by 60-120 in), and its description says 'It can grow up to 6 to 12 feet tall, 5-10 feet wide'; no admissible page gives an indoor or container figure. The width is nulled with the height because both come from that one outdoor block. RHS's Max Height is '2.5-4 metres' (98.4-157.5 in) and its Max Spread '0.5-1 metres' (19.7-39.4 in), so the two pages disagree on spread; its description reads 'A tender, slow-growing architectural, succulent shrub producing very upright stems and branches to 1.8m (6ft) high.', a general figure that the same paragraph sets apart from plants 'grown in the home' (flowers 'unlikely to be produced on plants when grown in the home'), so it is not an indoor figure either. The research record had landed 72-144 in by 60-120 in.

Fertilizer, humidity, light foot-candle values: no admissible source stated them. Spines/latex handling is in toxicity_detail. NC State notes the plant is potentially invasive in warm climates (naturalized in Cuba and India).

ASPCA (not an admissible source) has no entry for this species; its Pencil Cactus (Euphorbia tirucalli) entry was not used. Moved here from toxicity_detail at landing, since it rests on no admissible page.

That RHS field reads: 'Skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'. ASPCA (not an admissible source) has no F. microcarpa entry; its fig entries, Ficus benjamina and an unspecified Ficus sp., are listed toxic to dogs and cats and are not inherited here.

is_edible left null: no admissible source addresses eating the plant (NC State notes only that birds feed on the fruit).

humidity_need and humidity pct left null: NC State says 'High humidity (70% - 100%) is preferable and seems to favor the development of aerial roots.', a preference rather than a requirement for that figure; its Description also says 'A tropical and subtropical species, the tree requires a warm climate and a humid atmosphere to thrive.', a climate requirement with no level or figure attached. soil_ph left null: RHS lists pH as acid or alkaline or neutral, so no ceiling or floor; NC State gives no pH.

soil_base left null: NC State's Soil Texture field reads High Organic Matter, an in-ground soil descriptor with no potting-mix token, and NC State mentions potting soil only as a rooting substrate for cuttings ('The species can be propagated easily by cuttings, either in water or directly in a substrate of sand or potting soil.'). water_regime and watering intervals left null: NC State's Moist tag is a soil adjective and no admissible source gives a watering statement; NC State only notes root rot can occur from overwatering.
Temperature fields left null: NC State says the tree is suitable for temperatures above 68 F all year, which is not a damage-onset or day/night range; RHS H1B is a UK hardiness rating.

RHS's Cultivation sentence allowing full sun or partial shade is genus-level Ficus text, identical on its Ficus benjamina and Ficus pumila pages, and is not used as species evidence.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Heptapleurum actinophyllum page). Page-top banner: "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." The Poison block sits under the heading "Poisonous to Humans:" and is human-scoped: Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: "All part of this plant are toxic if ingested. Oral irritation, pain and swelling of mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, and diarrhea. Skin irritation can result from contact with the sap of this plant." Poison Toxic Principle: Terpenoids, saponins, insoluble calcium oxalates. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The description warns: "All parts of this plant are toxic if ingested and should be kept out of the reach of pets and children. Skin irritation can result from contact with the plant's sap." Separate from the human-scoped Poison block, the Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs values support toxic_to_pets, and horses are listed as well. The same page's Uses (Ethnobotany) field reads "Used as animal food and as a medicine."; the page does not reconcile this with its Problem for Cats, Dogs and Horses values or its toxic-if-ingested warning, and no admissible source describes any human food use. records.name_note: Common names split across admissible sources. NC State's Dracaena angolensis page renders an alphabetized four-item Common Name(s) list, African Spear, Brazil Saint Bárbara Sword, Cylindrical Snake Plant and Spear Sansevieria, in the same order as its page title, and its description opens 'African spear is an easy-to-grow, succulent herbaceous perennial native to Africa.' MoBot's dedicated Dracaena angolensis page carries a single row reading 'Common Name: bowstring hemp'; its Noteworthy Characteristics prose, which still calls the plant Sansevieria cylindrica, says 'The common name bowstring hemp refers to the fibers that can be extracted from the foliage of some Sansevieria species.' RHS has no Dracaena angolensis page; its page filed under Sansevieria cylindrica renders the common name 'cylindrical mother-in-law's tongue' beneath its heading and lists 'African spear, cylindrical snake plant, spear sansevieria' under Other common names (that page is cited only for this name evidence and one handling warning). African Spear, the first entry of NC State's list and the name its description opens with, is used here; it is also the first of RHS's other common names, and it keeps the record off the bare 'Snake Plant', which belongs to Dracaena trifasciata (NC State's description of Dracaena trifasciata opens 'Snake plant is an erect, clumping, broadleaf evergreen, tropical herbaceous perennial in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae).' and its 'often confused with' module lists Dracaena angolensis; NC State's Dracaena angolensis page carries the matching 'is often confused with' module naming Dracaena trifasciata). Sansevieria cylindrica is the earlier name still used by MoBot's prose and RHS, and NC State lists it as a previous name. 'Boncel' (nicknamed the "starfish") is a cultivar per NC State, and braided or paint-tipped leaf cuttings are a sales form per NC State, not a separate taxon.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Poison Symptoms: 'Toxic if ingested by cats and dogs: dilated pupils, vomiting, stomach upset, abdominal pain, drooling, weakness, depression. Keep this plant away from pets and children. Humans should not ingest this plant. Skin irritation can occur from the plant sap.' Toxic principle: saponin. Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems. The severity rating is NC State's Poison Severity field, Low, under its human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading; the page-top banner restates it: 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' NC State's separate Problems list reads Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. 'Causes Contact Dermatitis' is marked No even though the Poison Symptoms text says skin irritation can occur from the plant sap. Tags on the page: #houseplant #easy to grow #interiorscape #problem for dogs #problem for cats #succulent #drought tolerant #problem for children #poisonous if ingested #th-touch. Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Succulent. RHS (Sansevieria cylindrica page, the name RHS files this plant under) separately says 'Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'; it gives no animal scope. No admissible source disagrees on scope. ASPCA's Sansevieria trifasciata entry was not used.
records.water_estimate_basis: NC State's species page: 'water only about every 2 weeks in summer and monthly in winter.' Only the literal '2 weeks' is converted (14 days); 'monthly' is a word cadence, so the dormant interval is left null.
unknowns: chill_damage_f left null: NC State says 'Bring it indoors when the temperature falls below 55 degrees Fahrenheit', which is a bring-indoors recommendation, not a stated damage-onset temperature; MoBot's hardy zones 10-11 are a hardiness rating, not an onset figure.

day/night temperature ranges, humidity_need and humidity percentages left null: no admissible source gives numbers or a humidity need (NC State's 'Humidity' under Resistance To Challenges is a tolerance trait, not a need; MoBot only says 'prefers warm locations').

light_fc_min, light_fc_good left null: no footcandle figures; NC State says 'Place it in a brightly lit window' and MoBot 'bright, indirect light and some full sun'. direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's species prose says only 'morning sun' outdoors; the 2-6 hours in its Light field is the site-wide category legend and was not used.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's structured Light field gives Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade (both mapped to part_shade). MoBot's structured Sun field gives 'Full sun to part shade' and RHS's Position (on its Sansevieria cylindrica page) gives Full sun, Partial shade, but full_sun is left out: NC State's Light field excludes it, NC State warns 'If taken outdoors in the summer, only give it morning sun to avoid sunburn.', and MoBot itself says 'Protect from hot afternoon sun.' and 'Indoor plants may be taken to shady outside locations in summer.'

soil_drainage left null: NC State's structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Occasionally Dry, Very Dry) and Soil Texture field (Sand, Shallow Rocky) do not by themselves call for sharp or gritty drainage; MoBot says 'evenly moist to dry, well-draining soil' and warns overwatering often causes root rot; no source gives a sharp/gritty requirement or a wet-tolerance statement that settles the scale.

water_regime left null: NC State gives only a cadence (about every 2 weeks in summer, monthly in winter) and MoBot says 'Water semi-regularly during the growing season, with significantly reduced watering from fall through winter' plus a structured Water field of 'Dry to medium'; no source states a dry-down rule. water_dry_down_target and water_check_depth_cm left null for the same reason. water_dormant_days_est left null because 'monthly' is a word cadence.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State and MoBot give no pH; RHS (Sansevieria cylindrica page) says 'Alkaline or Neutral' without a number.
fertilize_* fields left null: no admissible source page examined gives fertilizing advice for this species.
attracts_pollinators left null: NC State has no Attracts field and no source states pollinator use.
is_edible set false only on NC State's statement 'Humans should not ingest this plant' (and Poisonous to Humans listing); RHS says 'Harmful if eaten' on the synonym-name page.

RHS has no Dracaena angolensis page; its Sansevieria cylindrica page (Name Status 'Correct' there) was used only for name evidence and the handling warning, not for size, soil or sun. MoBot's Zone 10 to 11, height 4-6 ft and spread 1-2 ft were not used because NC State has its own Dimensions block (0 ft 6 in to 7 ft 0 in high, 0 ft 6 in to 2 ft 0 in wide) and is the anchor. Houseplant size rule: NC State's Dimensions figures stand, since neither bound exceeds 120 in and the page gives no separate indoor or container figure (its description says only that the leaves are 'up to 7 feet tall' and 'It will occasionally bloom in a container.').

MoBot plantfinder.mobot.org refuses non-browser clients from the cache tool, so its quotes were read in a browser and verify_quotes will SKIP them; the audit re-read every MoBot quote verbatim on the live page. The researcher did not check UF/IFAS, Clemson, Penn State, UMD or UGA for a dedicated page; an audit-time search of those domains surfaced none, only Penn State's multi-species article 'Snake Plant: A Forgiving, Low-maintenance Houseplant', which was not used.

common_name researched as 'Cylindrical Snake Plant' (the batch's working name); landed as 'African Spear'. The audit FLAGGED the researched value because no admissible dedicated page leads with it: it is the third entry of NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list and the second of RHS's Other common names, and the research had cited NC State's per-name alias page for it, whose H1 is only the name in its own URL. records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Opuntia microdasys page has no Poison block and no severity rating; its tag list carries "#non-toxic for cats" and "#non-toxic for dogs", alongside #contact dermatitis, #spines, #edible fruits, #houseplant, #cactus, #container plant and #perennial, and its Problems field lists "Contact Dermatitis" and "Spines/Thorns". RHS's dedicated Opuntia microdasys profile disagrees on dogs: its Potentially harmful field reads "Skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "Pets (dogs): Skin/eye irritant. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants" (the same entry appears on RHS's Opuntia ficus-indica and Opuntia robusta profiles). The hazard both pages describe is contact injury from the glochids, not poisoning; no source names cats as at risk. NC State's handling warnings: "The bristles are very thin, barbed, and will detach with the slightest touch." and "Wear protective gloves when handling this plant." Its Stem Description says the glochids "look cottony but are sharp, barbed and injurious". Plant Type values on the NC State page: Ground Cover, Houseplant, Perennial, Shrub, Succulent. Edibility statement, with its conditions: "Ripe fruit edible raw or in jelly. Pads can be eaten raw or cooked and have a mucilaginous texture. Remove spines and glochids from pads and fruit before eating." The genus-level ASPCA Tree Cactus (Opuntia species) entry was not used.

unknowns: RHS has a dedicated Opuntia microdasys profile at https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11881/opuntia-microdasys/details (Name Status: Correct); the www.rhs.org.uk/plants/opuntia-microdasys URL tried during research 404s because it lacks RHS's numeric plant ID. RHS gives 'bunny ears cactus' beneath its H1, Position 'Full sun' only, pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', Max Height '0.5-1 metres' (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread '0-0.1 metre' (0-3.9 in), and a Potentially harmful entry naming dogs (see toxicity_detail). NC State's species Dimensions block stays the size anchor, and NC State's Partial Shade light value is kept although RHS's Position field lists full sun only (RHS is not a North American source, so it does not exclude NC State's Partial Shade). RHS's Cultivation paragraph is genus boilerplate (identical on its Opuntia ficus-indica and Opuntia robusta profiles) and supplied nothing. Missouri Botanical Garden's PlantFinder (plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be reached (TLS certificate failure), so whether it has an O. microdasys profile is unverified.

toxic_to_pets: the two dedicated pages disagree on dogs. NC State tags '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' and has no Poison block or severity rating; RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Pets (dogs): Skin/eye irritant.' and, for people, 'Skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'. The hazard RHS names is contact irritation from the glochids, which NC State's #contact dermatitis tag, its Problems values (Contact Dermatitis, Spines/Thorns) and its glove warning describe for people; neither source describes poisoning, and no source names cats as at risk. Landed true at landing on RHS's dog line (the audit's recommended repair; b32 landed Opuntia ficus-indica true on the identical RHS entry), with NC State's tags kept as the disclosed counterpoint; the research value was false, which the audit removed.

is_edible is true only under conditions: ripe fruit eaten raw or in jelly, pads raw or cooked, and only after spines and glochids are removed from pads and fruit. Glochids are barbed, detach at the slightest touch, and NC State tags contact dermatitis.

soil_drainage fast: NC State calls for a fast-draining cactus potting mix to prevent root rot, a full dry-down between waterings, and its structured drainage values are Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, with no wet tolerance described. NC State's Resistance To Challenges lists Drought and Dry Soil.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the Acid band is open-ended, so no floor can be set; RHS's dedicated profile lists pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so alkaline soil is acceptable and no ceiling can be read off the closed top of NC State's Neutral band.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the species prose says only 'full sun to partial shade'; the hour ranges in the structured Light values are the site-wide light-category legend and were not used.

Winter 50-65 F figure is a cool-rest range only; no day/night temperature fields were filled. No chill-damage onset figure is stated: NC State says only that it is not frost tolerant and lists USDA Plant Hardiness Zone '9a, 9b, 10a, 11a, 11b', and RHS gives the bare hardiness rating 'H2'; neither is an onset temperature.
No fertilizer guidance on the NC State page; attracts_pollinators has no NC State Attracts field, so null. No watering day interval or check depth is stated, so those are null.
The alias 'Polka Dot Cactus' appears in NC State's list; it was not used as the common name and is not the same plant as Hypoestes 'Polka Dot Plant'.

NC State mature size (Dimensions block): Height 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. = 24-36 in; Width 4 ft. 0 in. - 5 ft. 0 in. = 48-60 in, matching its description ('This plant is slow-growing and will reach 2 to 3 feet tall and spread 4 to 5 feet as a mature plant.'). Houseplant size rule: no admissible page gives a separate indoor or container figure, and both are under 120 in, so they stand. RHS's 0.5-1 metres by 0-0.1 metre is not tied to indoor growing.
